root_idea.summary: A downward collapse or falling apart, especially when something loses its support.
root_idea.development: The physical image extends to the collapse of structures, banks, or wells, and figuratively to prostration, reckless plunging, and perishing. Related descriptions also apply the root to changes in darkness and winter, while one divergent usage conveys imputing something to someone.

senses.definition: To collapse, cave in, or fall into ruins.
senses.usage_conditions: In the Quranic construction فَانْهَارَ بِهِ, the structure or bank falls in and collapses with what is upon it.
In the Quranic phrase عَلَىٰ شَفَا جُرُفٍ هَارٍ, it describes a bank or cliff on the point of collapse.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To throw down, pull apart, or demolish a building; likewise to pull down an abrupt bank, its upper part, or the brink of a well.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Transitive physical usage, including the explicitly attested synonymous Form II expression هَوَّرَهُ.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To slay people and throw them down prostrate one upon another; to strike and prostrate an individual.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Figurative extension of throwing down, modeled on the falling of a bank or cliff.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To become thrown down, fall into ruins, or break into pieces; of a building or bank, also to crack without falling or to crack at the rear while remaining in place.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Intransitive usage; the source distinguishes complete collapse from structural cracking that leaves the object standing.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To plunge into affairs recklessly or venture into matters without adequate thought; a person in this state is rash and heedless of the consequences.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The verbal form describes the conduct or state, while مُتَهَوِّرٌ describes the person characterized by it.
Attested of a thing that comes to an end or is destroyed.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Of a building, bank, or well: fallen, falling, or cracked and structurally unsound, even if it has not yet completely fallen.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Broader adjectival usage covering instability and cracking beyond the Quranic bank expression.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A person weak or ineffectual in his affairs.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A figurative personal description likening lack of firmness to an unstable or collapsing well.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Of night, for its darkness to become intense.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A temporal usage applied specifically to the deepening of nighttime darkness.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Of night, for its darkness to break or recede.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A separately reported temporal interpretation, describing the darkness as if it had fallen away and passed.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Of winter, for most of its severity to pass.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Applied to the waning of the harshest part of the season.
The term is explained by the animals' number and tendency to fall upon one another.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To impute something to someone so as to make him suspected of it.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A rare divergent usage, explicitly distinguished from the principal falling and collapse branch.

lane_unit_coverage.note: Intransitive collapse and structural cracking branch.

Quran-attested collapsing adjective and broader structural-instability applications.

cautions: The Quranic nominal surface هَارٍ is presented under the normalized citation form هَائِرٌ; the evidence describes هَارٍ as a transposed form of هَائِرٌ.
Descriptions of تَهَوَّرَ الليل differ in the evidence: one gives intensifying darkness and another gives darkness breaking or receding; both are retained as distinct reported usages.
A historical Quran citation appearing in the adjectival lexical evidence is not converted into a modern verse location; the displayed Quran example uses the independently supplied QAC location 9:109.
